prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "JOHNSON & JOHNSON" (ticker JNJ), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "JNJ", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Johnson & Johnson
result.industry: Diversified healthcare: prescription medicines and medical devices
markets: Oncology medicines (multiple myeloma, prostate and lung cancer)
Immunology medicines (psoriasis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis)
Surgery devices (sutures, staplers, energy, surgical robotics)
Cardiovascular devices (electrophysiology, Abiomed heart pumps, Shockwave)
Vision (Acuvue contact lenses, cataract and refractive surgery)

mission.statement: At Johnson & Johnson, we blend heart, science and ingenuity to profoundly change the trajectory of health for humanity.
mission.plain: Use caring people, science and new ideas to make people around the world much healthier.

about.plain: Johnson & Johnson makes medicines and medical tools that doctors and hospitals use to treat sick people. Its medicines fight cancers like multiple myeloma, skin and gut diseases like psoriasis and Crohn's, and mental illnesses like depression. It also makes things surgeons use, such as stitches, staplers, artificial hips and knees, tiny heart pumps and contact lenses. In 2023 it spun off its shampoo and bandage business (now called Kenvue), so it now focuses only on medicines and medical devices.
about.customers: Hospitals, doctors, pharmacies, wholesalers and governments and insurers that pay for patients' treatments.
about.everyday: If you wear Acuvue contact lenses or know someone with a new hip or knee, there is a good chance J&J made it.

money.plain: Tremfya and Stelara for psoriasis and gut diseases
Artificial hips and knees, trauma and spine (DePuy Synthes)
Heart-rhythm ablation, Impella heart pumps, Shockwave
A soft-tissue surgical robot still in development and trials

result.summary: Yes. J&J has a wide moat built on a deep pipeline and patents in cancer and immunology medicines (Darzalex alone sold $14.4 billion in 2025), leading positions in several device markets, huge scale ($94.2 billion of 2025 sales) and an AAA credit rating that lets it buy innovation (Abiomed, Shockwave, Intra-Cellular). The advantage is product-by-product rather than permanent: patents expire, as the Stelara biosimilar collapse shows, so it must keep refilling the pipeline.

pricingPower.evidence: Patent-protected drugs like Darzalex (sales $14.35 billion in 2025) and Tremfya ($5.16 billion) keep premium prices, but once exclusivity ends prices collapse: Stelara fell to $6.08 billion in 2025 after US biosimilars arrived, and Medicare price negotiation under the Inflation Reduction Act covers Stelara, Xarelto and Imbruvica; device prices face hospital purchasing pressure and China volume-based procurement.

moats.evidence: Patents and regulatory exclusivity on medicines such as Darzalex Faspro, Tremfya, Carvykti and Rybrevant drive most profit, and the 140-year-old J&J name and Acuvue, Ethicon and DePuy Synthes brands are trusted by surgeons and doctors.

Surgeons trained on its orthopaedic, electrophysiology mapping (CARTO) and surgical systems, and patients stable on a biologic, tend not to switch, but rivals such as Boston Scientific's Farapulse have still taken electrophysiology share.
Little classic network effect; the CARTO mapping installed base and clinical data create only mild reinforcement.
With $94.2 billion of 2025 sales, $14.7 billion of R&D, 140,800 employees and 63 manufacturing plants, it can fund large trials and global launches few rivals can match.
Niche markets such as Impella heart pumps (Abiomed) and intravascular lithotripsy (Shockwave) have few competitors because they are small and need specialized trials and sales forces.
J&J is the incumbent; it does not have a business model rivals are unwilling to copy.
Decades of experience in biologics manufacturing, cell therapy (Carvykti with Legend) and running global late-stage trials is hard to replicate, though big pharma peers share similar skills.
Patent estates on daratumumab (Darzalex, licensed from Genmab), guselkumab (Tremfya) and amivantamab (Rybrevant) are exclusive assets for years, but each eventually expires.

customers.evidence: Doctors keep prescribing its leading drugs: Darzalex is the backbone of multiple myeloma treatment and Tremfya sales grew to $5.16 billion in 2025; hospitals buy repeatedly from Ethicon, DePuy Synthes and Biosense Webster, though talc lawsuits have dented consumer trust.

talent.evidence: J&J has 140,800 employees, appears regularly on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies and diversity/best-employer lists, and its scale and reputation help it recruit scientists and executives, though it is not seen as the top destination the way fast-growing biotechs are.

product.evidence: Darzalex is the standard antibody in multiple myeloma, Carvykti showed an overall survival benefit in CARTITUDE-4, and Tremfya has strong psoriasis, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's data including subcutaneous induction; in devices it leads in electrophysiology mapping but trails Boston Scientific's Farapulse in pulsed-field ablation and Intuitive in robotics.

competitors.name: AbbVie
competitors.note: Skyrizi and Rinvoq compete head-on with Tremfya and Stelara in psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease; Imbruvica shared with J&J.

competitors.name: Bristol Myers Squibb
competitors.note: Multiple myeloma (Revlimid, Pomalyst, Abecma CAR-T vs Carvykti) and schizophrenia (Cobenfy vs Invega).

competitors.name: Medtronic
competitors.note: Broadest device rival: surgery, spine, cardiac ablation (PulseSelect, Affera) and the Hugo surgical robot.

competitors.name: Boston Scientific
competitors.note: Farapulse pulsed-field ablation has taken share from J&J's electrophysiology business; also interventional cardiology vs Shockwave.

competitors.name: Abbott Laboratories
competitors.note: Electrophysiology (Volt PFA, EnSite mapping), structural heart and vascular devices.

competitors.name: Stryker
competitors.note: Hips, knees (Mako robot), trauma and spine versus DePuy Synthes.

competitors.name: Zimmer Biomet
competitors.note: Largest pure orthopaedics rival in hips and knees.

competitors.name: Intuitive Surgical
competitors.note: da Vinci robots dominate soft-tissue robotic surgery that J&J's Ottava aims to enter; also drives stapler and energy use.

competitors.name: Roche
competitors.note: Oncology (Columvi, Lunsumio bispecifics) and immunology; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Cosentyx competes with Tremfya and Stelara in psoriasis; Pluvicto vs Erleada in prostate cancer.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Elrexfio bispecific in multiple myeloma; Xtandi (with Astellas) vs Erleada in prostate cancer.

competitors.name: Sanofi
competitors.note: Sarclisa anti-CD38 antibody competes with Darzalex; Dupixent in inflammation.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Wezlana Stelara biosimilar, Otezla in psoriasis, and Imdelltra/Lumakras in lung cancer vs Rybrevant.

competitors.name: Alcon
competitors.note: Contact lenses and cataract/refractive surgery versus J&J Vision (Acuvue, Tecnis).

competitors.name: The Cooper Companies
competitors.note: CooperVision contact lenses compete with Acuvue.

threats: Stelara biosimilars (launched 2025) and Medicare price negotiation on Stelara, Xarelto and Imbruvica keep shrinking older drug sales
Darzalex is J&J's largest product (15% of 2025 sales); its key patents and Genmab licence-based exclusivity end around the early 2030s
Talc litigation: a proposed $5.5 billion ovarian-cancer settlement (July 2026) drove a one-time Q3 2026 charge that cut net earnings to $210 million; the deal needs 95% claimant participation
Boston Scientific's Farapulse pulsed-field ablation has taken share in electrophysiology, J&J's biggest device franchise ($5.6 billion in 2025)
Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci dominance makes the delayed Ottava robot a late entrant
Planned separation of the DePuy Synthes orthopaedics business adds execution risk
Tariffs, US most-favoured-nation drug pricing pressure and China volume-based procurement for devices

ceo.name: Joaquin Duato
ceo.background: Spanish-born veterinarian by training with an MBA from ESADE and an international management master's from Thunderbird; joined J&J in 1989 and ran its pharmaceutical business before becoming CEO (January 2022) and chairman (January 2023).

c1.evidence: J&J leads important fast-growing niches such as multiple myeloma (Darzalex $14.4 billion, Carvykti $1.9 billion in 2025), but its overall healthcare industry is mature and grew about 6% in 2025.

c2.evidence: Doctors pick J&J products for clinical data (Carvykti's overall survival benefit, Darzalex as the myeloma standard, Tremfya's IBD data), backed by patents, a $14.7 billion R&D budget and an AAA balance sheet that rivals find hard to copy, though each drug's edge lasts only until patent expiry.

c3.evidence: Nearly everyone recognises the Johnson & Johnson name (largely from baby shampoo and Band-Aid, now Kenvue's), but in its current fields it is one of several leaders rather than the single default like Intuitive in robotic surgery.

c4.evidence: Its Credo (1943) and purpose to 'profoundly change the trajectory of health for humanity' are emphasised constantly, but the company is run as a disciplined, profit-focused large corporation and its reputation has been hurt by talc and opioid litigation.

c6.evidence: “trusted, baby shampoo, big pharma, talc lawsuits” — the impression is mostly positive and long-standing, though litigation over talc and opioids has tarnished it.

c7.evidence: Global prescription medicines and medical devices are a multi-trillion-dollar market growing with ageing populations, and J&J's targets (cancer, immune disease, cardiovascular, neuroscience) are among the fastest-growing segments.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into neuroscience (Intra-Cellular Therapies' Caplyta, bought for about $14.6 billion in 2025), cardiovascular intervention (Abiomed, Shockwave) and soft-tissue robotic surgery (Ottava).

m1.evidence: Duato set a clear strategy to focus J&J on innovative medicines and medtech, spinning off Kenvue in 2023 and targeting double-digit growth by 2030, but he is a steady strategist rather than a visionary founder type.

m2.evidence: Duato is a career J&J executive (since 1989), not a founder; he manages with long-term stewardship but in a conventional corporate style.

m4.evidence: Duato frames leadership around Our Credo, which puts patients, doctors and employees before shareholders, but there is little distinctive evidence of servant leadership beyond that.

m5.evidence: J&J's decentralised, Credo-based culture predates Duato; he has sharpened it toward innovation (about 25% of 2025 sales from products launched in the past five years) but did not create it.

m6.evidence: Duato trained as a veterinarian and led the pharmaceutical business, so he understands science, but he is a commercial executive rather than an engineer or researcher.

m7.evidence: Duato emphasises the Credo and global health access, but under his leadership J&J pursued the controversial 'Texas two-step' bankruptcy strategy for talc claims, rejected by courts in 2023 and 2025.

m7b.evidence: No commencement address by Duato at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university is publicly reported.

m8b.evidence: Duato has a low-key, conventional executive style and is not widely known outside the industry.

m9.evidence: Under Duato sales from continuing operations grew from $79.99 billion (2022) to $94.19 billion (2025), with 2026 guidance of $101.0-101.4 billion despite Stelara's patent loss, and the Kenvue separation and Abiomed, Shockwave and Intra-Cellular deals were completed.

m10.evidence: J&J is known for financial discipline (AAA credit rating) but not for Bezos-style frugality; it spends heavily on marketing, administration ($23.7 billion in 2025) and acquisitions.

c10.evidence: Its medicines and devices reach patients worldwide, from Darzalex for myeloma and HIV drugs to sutures and contact lenses used by many millions of people every year.

p2.evidence: Discovering antibodies, CAR-T cell therapies and bispecifics and building heart pumps and surgical robots is extremely hard, highly regulated and important for human health.

f1.evidence: Sales from continuing operations rose every year: $78.74 billion (2021), $79.99 billion (2022), $85.16 billion (2023), $88.82 billion (2024) and $94.19 billion (2025).

f2.evidence: Gross margin slipped from 70.3% in 2021 to 67.9% in 2025 as the lower-margin MedTech business grew, and pre-tax margins have swung with litigation charges and gains.

f3.evidence: At 28 June 2026 debt was $49.0 billion against $20.8 billion of cash and securities, roughly 2.5 years of free cash flow (about $19.7 billion in 2025), with $85.0 billion of shareholders' equity and an AAA credit rating.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from about $21.2 billion (2022) to about $24.5 billion (2025), but reported pre-tax earnings swung widely ($19.4 billion in 2022, $15.1 billion in 2023, $16.7 billion in 2024, $32.6 billion in 2025) due to talc charges and reversals.

v1.evidence: Darzalex is clearly the standard of care in multiple myeloma, but across J&J's broad portfolio many products are one good option among several (e.g. Tremfya vs AbbVie's Skyrizi, its ablation catheters vs Farapulse).

v2.evidence: J&J regularly appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies and best-employer and diversity rankings, but it is not usually at the very top of 'best places to work' lists.

c5.evidence: Millions of cancer, psoriasis, Crohn's, schizophrenia and heart patients and the surgeons who rely on its sutures, implants and catheters would miss it, though rivals offer alternatives for many products.
